newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries steam higher on Election Day.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries steam higher on Election Day.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices steamed higher on Tuesday on a powerful fuel of hedge-fund and foreign buying and the market's expectations that Americans will re-elect President Bill Clinton and a Republican Congress.

"The markets think this election is not going to go haywire," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "They think that at a minimum, the Republicans will hold on to the Senate and that there will be checks and balances, accommodation, and that nothing wild will happen."
Long maturities scored the biggest gains, thanks partly to big purchases of 10-year notes by a well-known hedge fund, analysts said.

While three-, six- and year bill rates slipped a slight one, two, and three basis points to 5.02 percent, 5.07 percent and 5.13 percent, respectively, 10- and 30-year securities staged strong advances.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond finished at 102-4/32, up a full point to yield 6.59 percent versus Monday's closing yield of 6.66 percent.
Ten-year notes rose 18/32 to 101-22/32 to yield 6.27 pct.

"The market was already up more than a quarter of a point on very broadbased buying overnight when people came in to work in New York," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at CS First Boston.

Referring to the Treasury's three-part $38.5 billion quarterly refunding which began on Tuesday with the sale of $18.5 billion in three-year notes, Dimick said, "People who were short on a refunding trade got squeezed out, especially when rumors of a very large buyer of 10-years started swirling." Smaller speculative accounts augmented that activity, buying in the five-year sector, he said.
"Good foreign buying and the expected election results helped the market," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

"There's good foreign interest in our market still," said Moran. "That was apparent from the strength in the dollar we saw today." The dollar ended firmer versus the mark, yen, Swiss franc and British pound as traders bet that Republicans would retain their control of the U.S. Congress.
"There was a growing confidence that the government would be split between the Democrats and the Republicans which would be pleasing to the financial markets," Moran said.

While hedge fund and foreign buying and market optimism about the U.S. election drove prices higher, the market's performance was staged against a backdrop that has come to be viewed as very favorable for bonds.
"The buying is also a response to the great news from last week -- the (third-quarter Employment Cost Index) ECI, GDP (Gross Domestic Product) and the (October) employment reports," said Dimick.
"The economic fundamentals remain great for the markets," said Feinman. "We got the slowdown we needed and that the Federal Reserve expected and the market is reveling in it."
The market's only setback on Tuesday was a short-lived reaction to the results of the Treasury's $18.5 billion sale of three-year notes.

"The auction of the three-year notes was less than robust with the average interest rate about a basis point higher than expected and the volume of bidding a bit below average," said Moran. "The market dipped a bit when the auction results came out, but it rebounded later in the day.
Two-year notes rose three basis points to 100-9/32, up 3/32 to yield 5.72 percent.
